item.title: Quasiperiodicity breakdown and homoclinic bifurcations in the forced librations of a parametric oscillator
item.description: arXiv:2611.32278v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Above its instability threshold, a parametrically excited oscillator settles into one of two phase states. The response of these states to a second, much slower modulation of the same stiffness is investigated. In the rotating frame, this modulation periodically varies the detuning and drives the phase librations. When the modulation is slow compared with the libration frequency, the phase states follow adiabatically. As the two frequencies become comparable, this approximation breaks down and the driven libration resonates with the intrinsic one. This nonadiabatic regime is examined for a Duffing oscillator with nonlinear damping. The averaged equations describe a periodically perturbed planar system with integrable unperturbed dynamics, whose homoclinic loop is derived in closed form. The phase states persist as invariant tori supporting quasiperiodic motion. Their stability and period-doubling bifurcations are captured by a damped Mathieu equation, in which the modulation contributes to both parametric stiffness and parametric damping. A Melnikov analysis yields explicit thresholds for separatrix splitting and the onset of homoclinic intersections, which are corroborated by numerical computations of the invariant manifolds. Numerically it is revealed that these intersections arise well before sustained chaotic motion develops. The fate of the parametric oscillation depends markedly on the resonance condition: modulation at the libration frequency destroys the invariant tori and quenches the oscillation, whereas modulation at twice the libration frequency leaves it intact.
item.dc:creator: Pierpaolo Belardinelli

item.title: Torus breakdown and collective chaos in heterogeneously forced excitatory--inhibitory neural populations with cascaded synapses
item.description: arXiv:2611.32826v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Exact mean-field reductions of spiking networks provide low-dimensional descriptions of neural populations that are derived from the microscopic dynamics, rather than postulated phenomenologically. Here we extend the Montbri\'o--Paz\'o--Roxin framework to excitatory--inhibitory networks of quadratic integrate-and-fire neurons coupled through a double synaptic filter, in which every spike elicits a second-order (alpha-function) synaptic response. The reduction remains exact and yields an eight-dimensional system. A two-parameter bifurcation analysis in the mean excitabilities of both populations reveals nine dynamical regimes, organized by saddle-node, SNIC, Hopf and homoclinic bifurcations, a Bautin point and folds of cycles, including bistability between quiescence and collective oscillations, which we confirm with network simulations. We then periodically force the inhibitory population close to the homoclinic bifurcation, where the collective rhythm is slow and effectively two-dimensional. Weak forcing already produces quasiperiodicity, Arnold tongues and chaos, consistent with torus breakdown. Remarkably, forcing only a fraction $p$ of the inhibitory neurons with amplitude $A$ yields nearly the same dynamics, including the Lyapunov exponents, as forcing all of them with amplitude $pA$. We show that this equivalence follows from an exact rewriting of the reduced equations, with corrections of order $p(1-p)A^2$, and that heterogeneity guarantees the contraction between forced and unforced neurons, making it a generic property of heterogeneous mean-field populations.
item.dc:creator: Gonzalo Contreras-Aso, F. Javier Mar\'in-Rodr\'iguez, Gabriel B. Mindlin

item.title: Reconstructing hidden attractors with reservoir computing
item.description: arXiv:2611.22918v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hidden attractors are difficult to locate as their basins of attraction do not intersect with any small neighborhood of an equilibrium point. We examine the possibility of reconstructing the hidden chaotic attractor from time series via reservoir computing, where the reservoir is built by a network of driven Kuramoto oscillators. We compare all-to-all coupling, nearest-neighbour ring coupling, and a ring with one modified oscillator equation which ensures that any attractor will be hidden. The numerical results suggest that ring coupling supports accurate reconstruction over a wider range of coupling and forcing strengths than all-to-all coupling. Searches near reservoir equilibria nevertheless show why agreement in short-term prediction and long-term statistics does not establish preservation of hiddenness. Numerics for the modified ring show that it has the highest performance which coincides with our intuition that reconstructing the global dynamics would yield a more faithful attractor reconstruction. We also show that this construction precludes global forgetting of initial conditions for constant inputs, although local conditional contraction along a nonconstant signal remains possible. The distinction between reconstructing attractor dynamics and preserving basin structure provides a basis for evaluating and designing reservoir models of hidden attractors.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Zaman, Emel Khan, Thomas Geert de Jong
